question: A bank wants a streaming safety guard for its customer chatbot. How do HaloGuard 2.0 and PGuard each work, how accurate are they relative to dedicated guard models, what does PGuard add to serving cost, and what residual risks does HaloGuard report?

claims.text: HaloGuard 2.0 is an open streaming guard that scores every response token. Its English training data is constitution-derived synthetic data; its multilingual training uses PolyGuardMix, with harmful-onset supervision constructed during generation in Phase 2.

support.quote: Model: HaloGuard 2.0 (ours); Training data: constitution \to synthetic (English); PolyGuardMix (multilingual); Scored: every response token; Streaming: yes, open; Token supervision: onset constructed at generation (Phase 2)

claims.text: HaloGuard 2.0 learns a content boundary between encouraging harm and discussing harmful topics, and a temporal boundary identifying when the response contains enough evidence to intervene.

support.quote: The first is the content boundary, which works like input moderation and separates responses that encourage harm from those that just discuss harmful topics. The second is a temporal boundary, specific to streaming, that marks the point in a response where there is enough evidence to step in.
HaloGuard 2.0 builds on HaloGuard 1.0 by shifting from per-prompt decisions to per-token decisions in the model’s output.

evidence.text: SOTA Status. HaloGuard 2.0-0.8B is the strongest open streaming output guard in our comparison. Across six English response-safety benchmarks it reaches a macro F1 of 83.6 under one global streaming rule. That is 2.6 points above the best Qwen3Guard-Stream model (4B, 81.0) and 4.8 above the one closest in size (0.6B, 78.8). It is level with the strongest full-response guards, Qwen3Guard-Gen-4B and -8B (83.57), which see the complete response before deciding and have 5–10× more parameters. It is the best model on HarmBench (96.4) and on SafeRLHF (81.7, 11.2 points above the next model). Pooled over 12,347 responses it operates at 84.1 precision and 80.5 recall (FPR 14.3% , FNR 19.5% ), and its remaining error is mostly missed harm, concentrated on WildG. HaloGuard 2.0-Poly-0.8B reaches 83.1 response F1 on PolyGuardPrompts, macro-averaged over 17 languages. That is 5.0 points above Qwen3Guard-Gen-4B (78.1) and 7.3 above the strongest streaming guard, Qwen3Guard-Stream-8B (75.8), with a 6.1% FPR and 7.5% FNR. Its remaining headroom is in precision (75.5) rather than recall (92.5), and in Hindi and Thai. Together with HaloGuard 1.0, which leads the open input guards at 90.9 (0.8B) and 92.1 (4B) prompt F1, the 0.8B input and output guards form a complete moderation stack of 1.6B parameters. Evaluation scope. Three evaluations reported by recent guards are not part of this release. RTP-LX, as in HaloGuard 1.0, measures the toxicity of stand-alone utterances (insults, slurs, identity attacks). Our constitution does not treat that as harmful response content: a response that is rude but gives no harmful uplift is safe under our policy. For the same reason we do not use Shieldstral’s per-language results, which pool RTP-LX with PolyGuard

LlamaGuard framed moderation as instruction-following classification over a risk taxonomy and applied one model to both prompts and responses [ 13 ] . WildGuard introduced refusal detection as an additional output,
which is significant for response moderation because a refusal and a harmful completion may share the same prompt but require
opposite labels [ 7 ] .
ShieldGemma, NemoGuard and PolyGuard extended open moderation to new model
families, enterprise taxonomies and 17 languages [ 8 , 9 , 2 ] . More recent guards add reasoning or inference-time policies: OmniGuard reasons before
labelling [ 10 ] , while GPT-OSS-Safeguard, Nemotron-3.5-Safety and
Shieldstral accept a deployer-written policy at inference
time [ 12 , 11 , 4 ] .
All of them classify a completed response, so they must wait for generation to
finish before returning a verdict. Constitutional Classifiers (CCs) trained a streaming
output classifier that scores each token of a response and stops generation when
the harm estimate crosses a threshold [ 14 ] . The classifier
guards a frontier model and its weights are not public. Qwen3Guard-Stream attaches token-level classification heads to a Qwen3 backbone and
derives token labels by locating the first unsafe token of each unsafe response:
continuations are sampled from every prefix, scored by Qwen3Guard-Gen, and the
earliest prefix whose continuations are mostly unsafe is confirmed by an LLM
judge [ 3 ] . HaloGuard 2.0 is closest in shape to Qwen3Guard-Stream and closest
in data philosophy to CCs. It differs in how onsets are
obtained (in the corrective corpus they are constructed at generation time, so they
are exact rather than estimated), in how they are used (up-weighted in the loss and

time [ 12 , 11 , 4 ] .
All of them classify a completed response, so they must wait for generation to
finish before returning a verdict. Constitutional Classifiers (CCs) trained a streaming
output classifier that scores each token of a response and stops generation when

judge [ 3 ] . HaloGuard 2.0 is closest in shape to Qwen3Guard-Stream and closest
in data philosophy to CCs. It differs in how onsets are

evidence.text: HaloGuard 2.0 builds on HaloGuard 1.0 by shifting from per-prompt decisions to per-token decisions in the model’s output. The core rules stay the same, but now the system can look at both sides of each policy boundary, making it easier to see exactly where harm starts. The main idea is that a streaming guard needs to set two boundaries. The first is the content boundary, which works like input moderation and separates responses that encourage harm from those that just discuss harmful topics. The second is a temporal boundary, specific to streaming, that marks the point in a response where there is enough evidence to step in. If the guard is only trained on completions that are harmful from the start, it might miss this temporal boundary and focus only on the prompt. Comparing response pairs makes this issue clear. Adding a corrective training step with these pairs, and then averaging the model weights, raises the six-benchmark F1 score from 72.8 to 83.6. HaloGuard 2.0-Poly-0.8B (the multilingual version) uses the same training objective as PolyGuardMix and supports 17 languages, achieving an F1 of 83.1 on the PolyGuardPrompts response labels. Next up is finding training methods that maintain the streaming improvements during averaging. We also plan to try out larger models as the 0.8B version hasn’t been tried above that parameter count yet. In the future we’d like to look at conversation level scoring, category attribution, tool call scoring and joint evaluation of input and output guards on shared test concepts.
